title: Lineup Orders
statement: A relay coach wants to see every possible running order for a squad. Given distinct jersey numbers in players, return all orderings of them, listed in lexicographic order by number (compare first numbers, then second, and so on). An empty squad has exactly one ordering: the empty one.

hints.content: There are n! orderings, so the output itself is the dominant cost.
Build an ordering one position at a time, choosing any player not yet used.
If you try candidates in increasing order at every position, orderings come out in lexicographic order.
Sort the players first, keep a used[] array, and recurse; undo the choice after the recursive call.
Record a copy of the current ordering when it has n players.

solutions.title: Generate, then sort
solutions.intuition: Produce all orderings in any order and sort them at the end.
solutions.approach: perms(items) puts each item first followed by every ordering of the rest. Then sort the list lexicographically.
solutions.pseudocode:
perms([]) = [[]]; perms(items) = for each x: [x] + p for p in perms(items without x)
sort result lexicographically
commonMistakes: Sorting arrays with the default comparator, which compares them as strings.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Generating everything and sorting is simple, but the sort is unnecessary if generation follows the right order.

solutions.title: Backtracking over sorted players
solutions.intuition: Choosing positions left to right from a sorted list, smallest available first, enumerates orderings in lexicographic order.
solutions.approach: Sort the players. place() tries each unused index in order: mark it used, push it, recurse, then pop and unmark. Record a copy when the ordering is complete.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort players; place(): if |cur| == n: record copy; return
  for i: if not used[i]: used[i] = true; cur.push(p[i]); place(); cur.pop(); used[i] = false
commonMistakes: Recording current instead of a copy.
Forgetting to reset used[i] after recursing.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Backtracking with a used[] array builds each ordering position by position, and trying candidates in sorted order makes the output lexicographic without a final sort. Producing n! orderings of length n is the lower bound, so O(n! · n) is optimal here.
